subject: Known presence not captured in surveys

messages.author: 26a806861bc4d838
messages.subject: Known presence not captured in surveys
parts:
Hi all, 

I'm using a community model to investigate the relationship between occupancy of prairie-associated reptile and amphibian assemblages and some habitat/landscape covariates, and I have a conceptual question related to this. We're dealing with a tricky scenario where we failed to document some rare species at particular sites during our formal surveys, but they were haphazardly documented (either by us or by other trusted observers) at those sites during the study period. We'd like to incorporate those known presences to better inform our occupancy relationships, and I'm struggling to find a way to explicitly build that into the model. Does anyone have ideas/experience doing that, or, given that we're primarily interested in occupancy and not detection, should we simply count those outside detections as survey detections?

Thanks in advance for any advice,

Ethan Royal

messages.author: 00ebeb6e0521112d
messages.subject: Re: Known presence not captured in surveys
parts:
Dear Ethan,

I would believe that there are multiple ways of doing this, assuming you're using some BUGS software. One would be to simply declare the presence/absence state of those sites known. I.e. taking them out of the part of the model that goes like this:   z[i] ~ dbern(psi)

Instead for them you write this:    z[i] <- 1

I believe that another method might be to add these '1's' in a sort of special occasion in the detection history matrix, then not change anything in the model for the z's, but instead estimating a fully separate value of detection probability exclusively for this single occasion. This parameter would then not be estimable, and you wouldn't want to estimate it, but in this way you would still incorporate the information about the presences into the model. This method would probably also work with unmarked.

I'd be interested in whether others think that something in these ideas is wrong.

Best regards -- Marc

messages.author: 527d9b3ec7deff2d
messages.subject: Re: Known presence not captured in surveys
parts:
Hi guys, I agree with Marc about the second strategy.

I dabbled with this in a mark-recapture context, for example when known radio-tagged individuals were uncaptured during a sampling period.  What I did was include a separate likelihood to estimate a probability ("p.known") of being tagged, with an individual's "tagged" status as an observation of a Bernoulli variable (0/1):

tagged[i] ~ dbern(p.known * z[i])

This allowed those individuals to have a known z state of 1, despite having an all-zero capture history.  The "p.known" parameter is the proportion of N that is tagged.  This construct seemed to work fine under various simulations we explored.

In an occupancy context, "p.known" would be the proportion of occupied sites for species X that had an ancillary presence observation.  Obviously this parameter does not have any value in and of itself and only serves to inform the z states.

messages.author: 26a806861bc4d838
messages.subject: Re: Known presence not captured in surveys
parts:
Hi all,

Sorry for the delayed response, I wanted to spend some time working through your suggestions before returning.

Initially I played around with Marc's first suggestion just to see how it would turn out. Thomas Riecke was extremely helpful with that, and I got it to run with some very clumsily coded adjustments. Unfortunately the occupancy and species richness estimates it produced were wonky and I seemed to create as many problems as I was solving.

I've since been attempting to go the route Dan and Marc suggested by including a non-estimable z.known parameter based on auxiliary detections to inform z states for each species at each site. However I'm stuck on problems linking this parameter to the detection/occupancy processes. I'm using JAGS and have tried both in a simplified simulation model and in the community model code used for the full analysis (a modified version of the richness model from "Zipkin, DeWan, and Royle. 2009. Impacts of forest fragmentation on species richness: a hierarchical approach to community modelling") but I don't seem to have the modeling skills to make things work. I've exhausted my limited knowledge here, so if anyone has further suggestions or any example code they're willing to share I would be eternally grateful. I can share what I'm working with or provide details on study design if that would be helpful.

I really appreciate the advice and want to thank y'all for always being so helpful in this group.

Ethan

messages.subject: Re: Known presence not captured in surveys
parts:
Hey Ethan,

Firstly, did you try entering the known presences as data? So let's say z[i,t] is the latent occupancy of species i during time t. You're trying to estimate z[i,t] from the data. But for those species which were not detected but that you know were present, you turn z[i,t] for that species at that time to 1. You then feed this z[i,t] as an array (which is mostly NA except for the 1's with known presences) as data.

If you wanna go the other route, feel free to send me a script. I'm happy to have a play around with it.

Matt

Subject: Known presence not captured in surveys
 
Hi all, 

I'm using a community model to investigate the relationship between occupancy of prairie-associated reptile and amphibian assemblages and some habitat/landscape covariates, and I have a conceptual question related to this. We're dealing with a tricky scenario where we failed to document some rare species at particular sites during our formal surveys, but they were haphazardly documented (either by us or by other trusted observers) at those sites during the study period. We'd like to incorporate those known presences to better inform our occupancy relationships, and I'm struggling to find a way to explicitly build that into the model. Does anyone have ideas/experience doing that, or, given that we're primarily interested in occupancy and not detection, should we simply count those outside detections as survey detections?

Thanks in advance for any advice,

Ethan Royal
